endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: evaluate whether there are some individuals or groups who are systematically excluded from giving feedback due to language barriers or factors related to ability or access.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether evaluating feedback and incident-reporting channels for ability, language, or access barriers improves detection of AI harms in excluded groups, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement from the CHAI Responsible AI Guide.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The support comes from one framework source, which reflects expert consensus rather than measured effect.

The CHAI Responsible AI Guide lists this evaluation as a must, directing systems to check whether some individuals or groups are systematically excluded from giving feedback. This is a voluntary industry framework. The supplied material cites no FDA, ONC, civil-rights, or state statutory requirement that mandates it.

No supplied study examines who uses AI feedback or incident-reporting channels, so the evidence does not show whether patients with limited English proficiency, disabilities, low literacy, or limited digital access are underrepresented in these reports. The size of any gap remains unmeasured.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare the demographic and language profile of AI feedback and incident reports against the population served by the tool. Such studies would also need to test whether barrier audits, followed by changes such as interpreter-supported or non-digital reporting options, increase reporting from excluded groups and lead to earlier detection of harms.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, because no study was supplied at all. Health systems therefore have no empirical estimate of how often these groups are missed by current feedback channels or whether an evaluation would change that.
